column3: It supplies the immediate political premise: an invading ruler overturns a town's status and makes its mighty inhabitants humiliated.
A restored counterturn, resources, and a more numerous force illuminate the forceful reversal threatened here.
Mutual questioning offers only a distant public-confrontation parallel, without the ultimatum or subjugation.
Defeat ending in abasement closely clarifies the threatened reversal from resistance to humiliation.
The command to deliver the letter and observe their reply begins the exchange whose rejection reaches its ultimatum here.
Its contrast route and size terms do not clarify political humiliation or expulsion.
The inability of the calf to return speech gives only a remote use of return, not the command or threat here.
Solomon's refusal of the gift is the immediate cause of the return order and military threat.
Divine aid to a vulnerable group frames military strength as granted rather than self-sustained, but not the threatened expulsion.
It helps distinguish compelled political subordination from the focus's more total threat of expulsion and abasement.
The channel-level resource-transfer material does not identify an element of the ultimatum.
It directly presents opposition ending among the most abased, though without the focus's military and territorial action.
Destroyed generations that do not return offer only a broad consequence parallel.
The queen's receipt of the noble letter starts the council process that leads to this response.
Loss of legal testimony is a different institutional penalty from the threatened political subjugation.
Voluntary humility toward parents contrasts with, but only faintly clarifies, compelled humiliation.
The proposed gift and awaited return of its envoys directly establish the diplomatic test rejected before this threat.
Threatened abasement under coercion offers a distant status-loss parallel in a different scene.
The command to return one's gaze with it humbled is a limited verbal and outcome parallel.
The channel resonance does not localize a useful contribution to the focus scene.
Those seeking an elevated religious status are struck with humiliation, clarifying reversal of pretension but not expulsion.
The arrogance of a ruler and his troops, followed by their return for judgment, parallels the exposure of proud force.
It identifies Solomon as the sender and grounds the authority of the preceding letter.
Divine independence from weakness supplies only a broad sovereignty backdrop to Solomon's claim of superior power.
The garden reward has no material link to the ultimatum, army, or expulsion.
Qarun's wealth and exultation faintly contrast with the gift that Solomon rejects, but add no military outcome.
Visible abasement as an enveloping condition clarifies the force of the promised humiliation.
The bare mention of Iblis's troops adds only a generic military collective.
The letter's command not to exalt themselves and to come submitting states the voluntary alternative to the later forced abasement.
The demand for a direct encounter does not clarify the diplomatic ultimatum or its consequence.
Its claim that the mighty will expel the lowly directly parallels the focus's expulsion-and-status language while exposing contested claims to honor.
Solomon's severe disciplinary alternatives show his authority, but not the diplomatic or military sequence.
Worldly humiliation imposed for arrogant false devotion reinforces the reversal from claimed elevation to disgrace.
Divine support with unseen forces and the lowering of opponents' word closely frames authoritative victory over resistance.
Selection, repentance, and guidance do not add to the threat of force or expulsion.
Refused voluntary prostration followed by abasement clarifies the distinction between willing submission and humiliating compulsion.
Worldly recompense and adornment do not clarify the focus action.
The queen's consultation explains the deliberative stage immediately before the gift and ultimatum.
Subdued fruit describes ease of access, not human abasement.
The dispute over the Hour does not illuminate the military response.
Its worship and charity description does not clarify this narrative threat.
Garments and mutual facing do not add to the focus scene.
Pharaoh's threatened expulsion of a city's people supplies a tyrannical territorial coercion parallel.
Turning from a messenger and responding to mercy gives only a general refusal backdrop.
Coming out to petitioners is unrelated to expelling a defeated party.
The council's claim of strength and severe martial power is the immediate human alternative considered before the gift strategy.
A messenger being told to return supplies a different but limited envoy-return parallel.
The next command acts before their arrival in submission, showing the authority's concrete preparation after the ultimatum.
Return to people with an interpretation is unrelated to the threatened return and invasion.
Material provision does not clarify the gift refusal or military outcome.
Gentleness toward believers and strength against disbelievers offer a contrasting kind of status relation, without this coercive sequence.
The powerful agent's offer to bring the throne develops the authority and capability invoked immediately after the threat.
Its references to coming food and leaving a creed do not clarify the focus.
The sign of the radiant hand has no material relation to army, expulsion, or abasement.
It makes warning precede abasement and disgrace, supporting the ultimatum's warning function.
The ordered gathering of Solomon's forces directly specifies the army named in the threat.
Repeated exclusion from the Fire gives a distant coercive-containment parallel, not territorial expulsion.
The call to worship and obey gives only the voluntary-obedience side of the focus's submission contrast.
Hope for replacement after loss does not clarify the ultimatum.
Ignorance of the Hereafter does not add to the military or diplomatic action.
Humble prostration without arrogance provides a faint voluntary alternative to forced abasement.
The command to eat lawful things and act rightly does not illuminate the focus.
The command to leave because of arrogance, ending among the abased, closely joins expulsion to humiliation.
Faces cast into the Fire show punitive reversal, but not the focus's political or territorial action.
The assertion that the divine host prevails reinforces the focus's claim of irresistible forces, though it is generic.
The number of guardians does not add a localized military or status parallel.
Offering food to guests does not clarify the refused gift or threat.
Proud denial despite inward certainty and its ruin provide a same-surah pattern of arrogant resistance meeting consequence.
The bare reference to armies contributes only the most general military association.
Persistent refusal and arrogance provide a distant resistance pattern, without the focus's forceful response.
Following desire instead of belief does not clarify the scene.
All coming in abject submission at the blast provides a broader image of unavoidable, humbled arrival.
The spring of those brought near has no material connection to the focus.
Promises of wealth, children, gardens, and rivers do not clarify the ultimatum.
No ransom or ally at punishment faintly reinforces the futility of material escape, but not the scene's action.
The signs sent to Pharaoh's corrupt people provide only a remote authority-and-resistance backdrop.
The selected group's trembling and plea do not clarify the focus.
A warning before painful punishment offers a general precedent for the conditional threat.
An evident surviving sign after destruction gives only a broad consequence parallel.
The throne's rapid arrival and Solomon's attribution of it to divine favor complete the immediate authority sequence after the threat.
A lesser punishment intended to prompt return supplies a distant corrective-use-of-punishment parallel.
Turning away followed by destructive replacement of prosperity illustrates a consequence for refusal, though not military expulsion.
Faith and increased guidance do not clarify the focus.
Escalating signs and affliction aimed at return provide a general pattern of warning followed by coercive consequence.
The absence of prior books and warners does not illuminate the focus.
A party refuses to enter until powerful occupants leave, offering a territorial-force parallel without the focus's reversal.
The removal from gardens and springs depicts dispossession in a military narrative, though in the opposite direction.
The threat to expel messengers from the land directly parallels coercive territorial exclusion and its divine reversal.
Pharaoh follows with troops and is overwhelmed, giving a direct narrative of armed pursuit reversed upon the army.
Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops are shown what they feared, strongly illustrating the collapse of a dominant military order.
Honored people receiving fruit do not clarify humiliation, force, or expulsion.
The ruin of earlier, stronger peoples gives a broad warning that strength does not prevent reversal.
The prayer concerning burdens and forgiveness does not clarify the focus scene.
Family maintenance rules do not add to the ultimatum or its outcome.
Its penalties include exile and worldly disgrace, clarifying those outcomes but in a legal framework unlike the focus.
The absence of refuge does not add a specific connection beyond unavoidable consequence.
The prayer not to become a trial for oppressors does not clarify the focus action.
The call to strive and submit supplies only a voluntary sense of becoming Muslim, unlike the threatened compulsion.
Fasting boundaries and marital permission do not illuminate the focus.
Abundant fruit has no relevant connection.
The knowledge granted to David and Solomon establishes the divinely given authority behind Solomon's later ultimatum.
Solomon's inheritance and exceptional command over creatures provide the wider royal capacity presupposed by his threat.
The report of a queen with a great throne identifies the polity and royal status directly confronted by the letter.
Her people's sun worship explains the misdirected allegiance from which the later coming in submission departs.
Solomon's decision to test the envoy's truth directly precedes the letter, gift, refusal, and return command.
The order to alter the throne advances the authority's response from threatened force to a test of recognition.
The queen's response before the altered throne shows the encounter moving toward acknowledgment rather than the threatened invasion.
Her prior worship had barred her from guidance, clarifying what makes her eventual submission a changed stance.
Her explicit submission with Solomon supplies the realized voluntary alternative to the focus's threatened forced abasement.
Solomon's prayer for an unmatched dominion directly frames the exceptional authority exercised in the focus scene.
The subjugated wind illustrates a divinely controlled force available to Solomon, though not this diplomatic action.
The devils made subject to Solomon expand the scale of the forces under his command.
Others bound in chains reinforce the dominion and coercive capacity surrounding Solomon's rule.
A divinely sent force of great might entering homes closely parallels an irresistible army entering a resistant polity.
The later entry and destruction after disobedience closely joins military return, penetration of a place, and reversal.
The expulsion of a resistant community from their homes directly illuminates territorial removal, though in another historical setting.
The call to fight a people of great might until they submit parallels the focus's alternative between resistance and submission.
An army facing Goliath and the admission of having no strength against him sharply echoes the focus's claim of forces they cannot resist.
The prayer for steadfastness and victory when meeting a hostile force supplies the reciprocal battlefield perspective on irresistible power.
The command to prepare force gives a general military-capability backdrop but not the focus's diplomatic or humiliating outcome.
The wind subjected to Solomon supplies another account of exceptional divinely granted capacity behind his authority.
The devils working for Solomon further specifies the nonordinary forces associated with his dominion.
Solomon's command over the wind and productive forces reinforces the divinely granted resources behind his assertion of superiority.
The jinn working under Solomon's direction broadly supports the scale of his rule without adding the ultimatum's outcome.
